1.pericope_label: In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, which was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans
debates: Which Darius is meant, and what hangs on the answer
From what date the seventy years are to be counted
Whether a promise already given makes prayer needless
outliers: Ellicott lays out three separate seventy-year spans that can be marked off in the captivity, and says Daniel could not be sure which was his
Clarke argues from Daniel possessing the scroll that the prophecies had already been collected and preserved as inspired
Keil and Delitzsch reports the modern verdict that the prayer is assembled out of older prayers
themes: A prime minister who still had time for his Bible
A window still turned toward a ruined city
A promise read as a summons to pray harder
One word carried over from an older scroll

3.pericope_label: And I set my face unto the Lord God, to seek by prayer and supplications, with fasting, and sackcloth, and ashes
debates: Whether setting the face means turning toward Jerusalem or simply looking to God
Why a confession of sin has to come before a request for pardon
How the dreadfulness of God and the nearness of the covenant stand together
outliers: Calvin says the earlier turning toward Jerusalem was a claim of possession on the holy land, not a way of praying
Ellicott finds the closest parallel to this prayer outside the canon rather than in Ezra or Nehemiah
Calvin observes that the opening title puts an obstacle in the suppliant own way
themes: A window habit kept when the penalty was death
An exile claiming his land by a gesture
Mercy kept beyond what the covenant required
A God whose holiness drives back the one who names it

5.pericope_label: We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even by departing from thy precepts and from thy judgments
debates: How the four verbs of confession divide, if they divide at all
Who is covered by the list of those the prophets addressed
Whether the pairing of commandments and judgments is mere repetition
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch shews three of the four words already fixed as a formula by Solomon and the psalmist, with Daniel adding the fourth
Calvin refuses to divide the verbs and reads the pile-up as a goad to a penitence that comes hard
Calvin says the law leaves the offender no defence though he had the eloquence of all the rhetoricians
themes: A confession made in the plural by a man who had earned none of it
Sins recalled but their weight quietly reduced
Stumbling at noon with the lamp still lit
Warnings sent to kings and to the whole land alike

7.pericope_label: O Lord, righteousness belongeth unto thee, but unto us confusion of faces, as at this day
debates: Whether the word means Gods righteous cause or his righteousness itself
Whether guilt can be measured by the severity of the punishment
Why the confession of shame is repeated a second time
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch rejects the softened rendering thine was the righteous cause as an arbitrary interpolation
Ellicott hears the prophet drift unconsciously toward the promise of the root of Jesse while still confessing
Calvin says those God punished least were not the least guilty
themes: Shame that shews itself in the face
Glory that only appears when every mouth is stopped
A lighter hand that is no acquittal
Kings who exempt themselves from ordinary law

9.pericope_label: To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgivenesses, though we have rebelled against him
debates: Whether the curse is poured like rain or like molten metal on a condemned man
Whether the word for law here means the law of Moses or teaching at large
Why a confession of sin is useless without the hope of pardon
outliers: Clarke reads the verb from a method of execution, pouring molten metal on the criminal
Calvin names two opposite dangers, torpid security and a sorrow that absorbs the mind, and says both come from the same quarter
Ellicott says the threatenings had already been partly fulfilled once, and that Daniel is seeing the whole of them
themes: A fountain with many streams running from it
Confession that ends in an abyss for want of hope
Faults in a neighbour that are crimes in a son
A curse falling like rain and burning like silver in the fire

12.pericope_label: And he hath confirmed his words, which he spake against us, and against our judges that judged us, by bringing upon us a great evil
debates: Whether watched means hastened, waited for an opening, or kept a standing guard
Who the judges are, and whether the failure was theirs or the people
Why a punishment that fell exactly as foretold changed nobody
outliers: Calvin explicitly rejects the reading that makes the verb mean haste, and takes it of a sentry on duty night and day
Gill reports the almond tree as named from the same root, because it blossoms before the other trees
Ellicott turns the verb into the ground of the petition, since the same prophet who foretold the curse promised the release
themes: Threats that turn out not to have been scarecrows
A word borne aloft over a people lying flat
Prayer offered in quantity and refused for formality
A sentence held in suspense so that it may not have to fall

15.pericope_label: And now, O Lord our God, that hast brought thy people forth out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and hast gotten thee renown
debates: Whether the righteousness appealed to is justice, faithfulness or plain kindness
Why the deliverance from Egypt is the ground of a request about a later exile
What the word all is doing in the appeal
outliers: Calvin says those who read the word as judgment are inexperienced interpreters, since they set Gods justice against his pity
Keil and Delitzsch refuses to let the same word soften into grace, and keeps it as proofs of righteousness
Keil and Delitzsch quotes Jerome approvingly and then says the remark does not go deep enough
themes: An old rescue treated as a standing undertaking
A shield the faithful reach for when they fear abandonment
A plea that names no merit at all
Sins enough to drown a people, set against mercies

17.pericope_label: Now therefore, O our God, hear the prayer of thy servant, and his supplications, and cause thy face to shine upon thy sanctuary that is desolate
debates: Whether for the Lord sake means for the Messiah or because God is Lord
Why the answer was withheld through seventy years of asking
What it means for a name to be named over a city
outliers: Calvin reads the piled-up petitions as fervour rather than eloquence, and distinguishes them from the heaped words of hypocrites
Keil and Delitzsch refuses the rendering named after thy name as enfeebling the expression
Calvin says the delay is caused at our end, our coldness interposing between us and the ear of God
themes: Doubt that shuts a door already open
Words that seemed for seventy years to be spoken to the deaf
A private prayer deliberately made public
A ruin that argues for its own repair

20.pericope_label: And whiles I was speaking, and praying, and confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel
debates: Whether the angel was made to fly swiftly or came in weariness
How a man who had seen no altar for seventy years still reckons by the evening sacrifice
Why this prayer was answered before it was finished
outliers: Ellicott reports a marginal rendering that would refer the weariness to Daniel own body rather than to the angel flight
Calvin says we should not be surprised at unanswered prayer, since our best praying has a hundredth of this zeal
Calvin makes the ruined altar an argument for keeping a sacrament in mind when it cannot be received
themes: An answer that arrives before the knees are off the ground
A great man still with sins of his own to name
An hour kept by men who had no altar
A daybreak measured against a morning star

22.pericope_label: And he informed me, and talked with me, and said, O Daniel, I am now come forth to give thee skill and understanding
debates: What the perplexity was that the angel came to relieve
Whether the commandment that went forth looks back to a decree or forward to the revelation
How a decree already fixed can still be granted in answer to prayer
outliers: Ellicott states the hinge plainly, that the seventy in question are weeks to come rather than the years already spent
Calvin says the decree went forth as a prince decree does, being published rather than made
Gill notes that more was revealed than had been asked for, and none of it owed to the merit of the asking
themes: An angel assigned as a private tutor
A heart opened by the making known of secrets
A decree issued the moment the praying stopped
A title of love given to one man and matched in another

24.pericope_label: Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city, to finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins
debates: Whether the weeks are weeks of days or of years, and why the figure is used at all
Whether sealing up vision means fulfilling prophecy or ending it
Whether the most Holy is a place, a thing, or a person
outliers: Calvin says no one on his own side has explained why years are counted in weeks, and answers that it sets seventy weeks against seventy years
Ellicott judges the marginal readings of the first and fifth clauses to be conjectures of early critics rather than original text
Clarke notes the answer given is not the answer asked for, the captivity in question being a different one
themes: A number cut out of time and set aside
Seventy years of darkness answered by seven times as long of light
Prophecy sealed up because it has nothing left to say
A holiness that turns out to be a person

25.pericope_label: Know therefore and understand, that from the going forth of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem unto the Messiah the Prince shall be seven weeks, and threescore and two weeks
debates: Where the sentence divides, and whether the accent after seven weeks is to be trusted
Which decree the reckoning starts from
Whether the anointed prince is a person of that day or the Messiah
outliers: Ellicott rejects the received Hebrew accentuation here; Keil and Delitzsch defends the same accents as right
Clarke counts the four hundred and ninety years backwards from the death of Christ to find the decree
Ellicott says the word rendered wall cannot be made out at all, and reports only what its etymology suggests
themes: Seven weeks cut off before sixty-two are counted
A number counted backwards to find its own beginning
A title of leader that neither adds nor takes away a crown
Walls raised in one long tale of opposition

26.pericope_label: And after threescore and two weeks shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself: and the people of the prince that shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary
debates: What the words but not for himself actually say
Who the coming prince is, and whether he has appeared earlier in the book
Whether the cutting off begins the seventieth week or merely falls within it
outliers: Ellicott says the destruction is laid to the people and not to the prince at all
Calvin lists three readings of the obscure clause and calls them all too frigid before giving his own
Ellicott reports a reading in which what is cut off is not a person but an unction
themes: A number that resolves into seven, sixty-two and one
A clause that says only he has not, and stops
Troubled times that spill past the years assigned them
A destruction credited to an army rather than its general

27.pericope_label: And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease
debates: Who confirms the covenant, and whether the subject is a person, a week, or the covenant itself
Whether the received Hebrew text of the abomination clause can be construed at all
What the wing of abominations means
outliers: Gill refuses the messianic reading on a purely chronological ground, that the covenant of grace is not confirmed for a week but for ever
Clarke rests the clause on a thirteenth-century manuscript reading that removes the difficulty altogether
Ellicott says the familiar Greek sense cannot be got from the Hebrew without dropping a letter and changing a vowel
themes: A subject the grammar declines to name
A covenant written on flesh instead of stone
A desolator riding on wings as God rides on the wind
One letter standing between two readings of a prophecy
